title: Nested and Local Classes
relevance: Tests whether candidates understand C++ nested/local classes as scoping and encapsulation tools, including the no-implicit-outer-instance rule versus Java and the access and local-class restrictions that trip people up in OAs and interviews.

phases.goal: Establish what nested and local classes are and why they exist for scoping and encapsulation.

must_hit.point: A nested class is a class declared inside another class; it is a member of the enclosing class for scoping and obeys public/private/protected access control.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says nested class lives in the outer class scope and is subject to the same access rules as other members.

must_hit.point: Typical use is hiding a tightly coupled helper type (e.g. a list node or container iterator) so it does not pollute the global namespace.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions Node-in-LinkedList or Iterator-in-container style helpers kept out of the global namespace.

must_hit.point: A public nested class is used from outside via Outer::Inner with the scope resolution operator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives Outer::Inner / Container::Iterator qualification as the way external code names the type.

must_hit.point: A local class is defined entirely inside a function body and is visible only in that function block.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes a class declared inside a function and usable only there, for tiny throwaway objects.

probes: What is a nested class in C++, and how does a local class differ?
When would you nest a helper type like a node or iterator inside a container class?

hints.1: Think about where the class name is visible and what problem nesting solves.
hints.2: Contrast a class declared inside another class with one declared inside a function.
hints.3: Nested class: member of outer for scoping/access; local class: only inside that function; both mainly for encapsulation/scoping.

phases.goal: Pin down instance relationship, access rights, out-of-class definition, and local-class restrictions.

must_hit.point: Unlike Java inner classes, a C++ nested class has no implicit outer instance; it is an entirely separate object type with no automatic this to the enclosing object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly contrasts with Java and says there is no implicit link or outer this.

must_hit.point: A nested class does not get special access to the outer class's non-static members; to use outer object state you must explicitly pass a pointer or reference to the outer object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says you pass Outer* or Outer& yourself; no automatic outer instance access.

must_hit.point: You can forward-declare a nested class inside the outer class and define its body later outside using Outer::Inner syntax.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes forward declare inside, then class Outer::Inner { ... }; outside.

must_hit.point: As a member, a nested class has access rights to the outer class's private members (e.g. private statics or typedefs), but still cannot read an outer object's private non-static data without an explicit outer object reference.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Splits language access rights from instance: can touch private statics/typedefs; needs an outer object to touch non-static private data.

must_hit.point: Local classes cannot access non-static local variables of the enclosing function, cannot have static data members, and have limited linkage.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those three restrictions on local classes.

probes: Does a C++ nested class have an implicit pointer to an instance of the outer class?
Can a nested class access the outer class's private members? Can a local class capture locals?

hints.1: Compare C++ nested classes to Java inner classes on the outer-instance link.
hints.2: Separate type-level membership/access rights from needing an outer object instance.
hints.3: No implicit outer instance—pass Outer*/&; member access rights yes for privates like statics/typedefs, but non-static instance data needs an explicit outer reference; local classes cannot use non-static locals, have no static data members, limited linkage.

phases.goal: Cover when nesting helps, when it costs nothing, and why local classes lost to lambdas.

must_hit.point: A nested class is only a type declaration and does not increase sizeof of the outer class unless the outer class declares a data member of that nested type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says nesting itself is free; only a member of that type affects the outer object's footprint.

must_hit.point: Local classes are rarely used today because of their severe restrictions and because modern lambda expressions cover the tiny throwaway-object use case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links rarity to restrictions plus lambdas replacing the niche.

must_hit.point: Defining a nested class body outside the outer class (after a forward declaration) can keep the enclosing class definition cleaner.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions cleaner outer class by forward-declaring inside and defining Outer::Inner outside.

probes: Do nested classes cost memory on the outer object?
Why are local classes uncommon in modern C++?

hints.1: Ask whether nesting a type adds fields by itself.
hints.2: Type nested inside vs data member of that type; local class limits vs lambdas.
hints.3: No sizeof impact unless you store a nested-type member; local classes are restricted and largely replaced by lambdas; out-of-line Outer::Inner definition can tidy the outer class.

phases.goal: Apply nested/local classes to concrete container and function-local patterns from the material.

must_hit.point: In a LinkedList, a private nested Node with data/next keeps the node type hidden while the list holds a Node* head and constructs nodes inside methods like append.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes private nested Node used only by LinkedList internals.

must_hit.point: A public nested Iterator (e.g. Container::Iterator) is the pattern for exposing a related type that clients must qualify with the outer name.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names Container::Iterator or similar public nested helper clients instantiate with Outer::.

must_hit.point: A local class inside a function (e.g. Processor inside processData) is appropriate only for a tiny type used solely in that function block.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a function-local class instantiated and used only inside that function.

probes: Show how you would hide a list node type using a nested class.
How would a client create a public nested iterator type?

hints.1: Pick a container helper that should not be a global type.
hints.2: Private nested Node vs public nested Iterator vs class inside a function.
hints.3: private class Node inside LinkedList; client uses Container::Iterator; local Processor only inside processData.

tradeoffs.topic: Nested type declaration vs nested-type data member
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Nesting only introduces a scoped type and does not grow the outer object's sizeof; sizeof grows only if the outer class actually declares a data member of that nested type.
Local classes can make tiny throwaway types, but they cannot access non-static locals, cannot have static data members, and have limited linkage—so lambdas largely replace them in practice.

tradeoffs.topic: Define nested class inside vs outside the outer class
tradeoffs.strong_answer: You can keep a forward declaration inside the outer class and define Outer::Inner later outside for a cleaner enclosing class definition.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a C++ nested class is like a Java inner class with an implicit outer instance.
gotchas.correction: A C++ nested class has no implicit outer instance and no automatic this to the enclosing object; pass an outer pointer or reference explicitly if needed.

gotchas.trap: Thinking nested classes always increase the outer class's memory footprint.
gotchas.correction: A nested class is a type declaration only; it does not affect sizeof of the outer class unless the outer class declares a data member of that nested type.

gotchas.trap: Answering yes or no flatly to whether a nested class can access the outer's privates.
gotchas.correction: As a member it has access rights to outer privates (e.g. private statics or typedefs), but without an outer object reference it still cannot read that object's private non-static data.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a local class to use the enclosing function's non-static local variables or to have static data members.
gotchas.correction: Local classes cannot access non-static locals of the enclosing function, cannot have static data members, and have limited linkage.
